entities.summary:
Jordanes, also written as Jordanis or Jornandes, was a 6th-century Eastern Roman bureaucrat of Gothic descent who became a historian later in life. Born of unknown parentage, Jordanes served under Emperor Justinian II, where he became familiar with the intricacies of Byzantine politics and the complexities of the Eastern Roman Empire. He later traveled to Italy and became a prominent historian, penning the works of the Roman historian Cassiodorus and incorporating elements of Gothic history into his own narratives. Jordanes' significance lies in his unique blend of Eastern Roman and Gothic perspectives, offering a rare glimpse into the cultural dynamics of the late Roman Empire.

Jordanes' most famous work, the 'Getica', chronicles the history of the Goths from their origins in Scandinavia to their migrations across Europe. The work is notable for its inclusion of Gothic traditions and its attempt to bridge the cultural divide between the Eastern Roman and Gothic worlds. Jordanes' historical significance extends beyond his own work, as his writings served as a model for later historians and helped to shape the development of Gothic identity in Europe.

The legacy of Jordanes can be seen in the continued study of Gothic history and culture, as well as the ongoing influence of his works on the development of historiography in the Byzantine Empire. His writings have also been subject to scholarly debate and reinterpretation, with some historians arguing that his work reflects a deliberate attempt to promote a unified Gothic identity.

In the 17th century, Jordanes' works were rediscovered by European scholars, who saw in them a valuable window into the cultural history of the Eastern Roman Empire. Today, Jordanes is recognized as a significant figure in the history of Byzantine and Gothic studies, his works continuing to be studied and debated by scholars around the world.
